An Account of Master Boting Ciyun’s Seventieth Birthday (Autograph of Actual Practice).
In the summer of the Gengchen year, he sought seclusion among the springs and rocks north of Longgang. The mountains and rivers were lush and verdant, shaded by pines and bamboos.
The mist cleared; light clouds drifted far away, and several birds came slowly. Suddenly, it was as if he had forgotten his very life, unaware that he was in the human world.
On the third day of the third month of the Chongshou era, Wenshu rose from his seat and knelt, saying, "I, Wenshu, have been attending you for many years.

I pray that you will reveal the beginning and end of your own circumstances regarding leaving the household life and studying the Way. Would it not be of great benefit for later students to hear this? Thereupon, [the Master] spoke in sixty verses.

In the *Jiǎ* year, I compiled the *Nianpu* (Chronological Biography) and exhorted him [to write it]. Now, seventy years have passed; I have again appended events from the past decade as supplementary additions, so that those who read it shall not feel any regret.
My surname is Shen; I am a native of Tíngxī in Rénhé. My father’s name was Xiāng, and my mother was of the Zhāng clan.
He was born on the eleventh day of the tenth month at the hour of Xu in the year of Xinsi, the fourteenth year of the Chongzhen era.

In the third year of the Shunzhi era, the year of Bingxu, when he was six years old, he was not drowned when swept away by water, not wounded when struck by bandits with blades, and not scorched when exposed to fire.

In the year Dinghai, at the age of seven, he saw a monk stroke his head and felt something extraordinary about it; he immediately resolved to leave the household life, but his mother would not permit it.

In Jichou, at the age of nine, he took leave of his parents and went to the city of Hangzhou to pay respects to the venerable master Ciyun Zuyuan as his teacher. His name was Xufa, and his courtesy name was Baiting.

At the age of eleven or twelve, he practiced the morning and evening liturgical recitations and the various rites for the sutras and repentance, extending his studies to the four [classes of literature].

He studied the *Book of Documents*, the *Book of Poetry*, and the *Book of Changes*. At the age of fourteen or fifteen, while assisting his master in renovating the Buddha hall, he would collect alms during the day to provide for the assembly, and at night he would prostrate before the Buddha and recite mantras.
In the year of Bingshen (1656), at sixteen, he shaved his head; at seventeen, eighteen, and nineteen, he took charge of the affairs of the monastery.

He renovated all the permanent images, scriptures, and ritual cloths, restoring them entirely to a new state. When these three years were nearly complete, in the winter of Jihai (1659), he took his leave.
The Master sought the precepts under the guidance of Master Huotang Yan of Nanping. On the first day of the full moon in the eleventh month, a carbuncle broke out on his abdomen.

He knelt before the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara) and recited the *Śūraṅgama-mantra* to pray for its healing. Within less than three days and nights, the poison was transformed into a simple sore and healed.
Thus, he was able to complete the Three-Altar Ordination rites. At the age of twenty, in the Gengzi year, he went to visit his former teacher, Master Deshui.
At age twenty-one, Master Yuan studied the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* under Chengshan; at twenty-two or twenty-three, he studied the *Vinaya-śāstra* under Tianzhu;

from twenty-four to twenty-five, he researched the various scriptural divisions of the masters of the Xian school; and at twenty-four or twenty-five, he studied the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* under Neiheng Dharma Master.

At Lianju, he studied the schools of *Xiang* (Characteristics) and *Xing* (Nature). Master Shengxian listened to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*; Master Lingcang listened to the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.
During the spring and summer of his twenty-sixth year, he went to Upper Zhi to listen to Master Laoshi’s lectures on the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*.

He also attended Stone Gong Heshang’s lectures on the *Huayan xuantan* and Jingchun Heshang’s lectures on the ritual procedures for the *Śatadāna-vidhi*. He re-edited the *Wujiaoyi* in six fascicles and requested correction.

The former master approved this, saying, "Your religious teachings and contemplative practices are now complete. He further established a vow to perform six *śrāddha* (feeding the hungry ghosts) rites every month and to transform food for the benefit of beings night after night.
In the eighth month of the twelfth lunar cycle of the Bingwu year of the Kangxi era, he received the robes and dharma from his teacher;
he was thus a fifth-generation descendant of Yunqi. He exhorted [his disciples] to thoroughly study the original texts of the sutras and treatises, and not...
I had been preoccupied with the various commentaries of different schools. On the full moon of the second month, I dreamed that a deity clad in golden armor said:

"At nineteen years of age, your hardships have already passed; this year, your hardships will end on your birthday. Consequently, I appended the *Rucika-dhāraṇī* one hundred and eight times after the *Śūraṅgama-mantra*.
Morning and night, amidst the interruptions of illness, I practiced without ceasing until my birthday. Suddenly, I dreamed of a monk who said: "It is fitting..."

If one recites the names of the three Buddhas—Śākyamuni, Bhaiṣajyaguru, and Amitābha—before the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, and adds the two mantras for Bhaiṣajyaguru and Rebirth after the *Sukhāvatī-vyūha Sūtra*, one may avoid the calamities of the thirty-third year.

Thereafter, if one performs these recitations morning and evening without fail, one may further style oneself "Anointed" (*abhiṣeka*). This is based on the instruction of my former teacher, who had thoroughly memorized the original text, and furthermore...

The *Śūraṅgama*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Avalokiteśvara-bodhisattva-paripṛcchā*, *Brahmajāla*, *Vajracchedikā*, *Bhaiṣajyaguru*, the *Avataṃsaka*’s "Names" and "Questions and Clarifications" chapters, the "Pure Conduct" and "Brahma Conduct" chapters, the "Chapter on the Secondary Marks and Vows" from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-kārikā*, the *Dharmadhātudarśana*, and the *Yichiriyebie* (One Day Five Leaves)—these he committed to memory with meticulous detail.
Three days were spent on one cycle of recitation, training them until they became his constant practice. Twenty.
89. Furthermore, he thoroughly investigated the various major scriptures of the three schools and recompiled their essential texts to prevent forgetfulness.

He also extracted and edited the *Wujiao yi kaimeng* (An Introduction to the Rituals of the Five Teachings) in one fascicle. In the spring of the ninth year of the Kangxi era, the Gengxu year, at the age of thirty, he arranged the *Wujiao jizheng tu* (Diagram of the Successive Realization of the Five Teachings).
At the request of many virtuous laypeople who offered robes as alms, he began lecturing on the *Prajñāpāramitā* at his own monastery during the Zhongyuan festival.

Jie. At the residence of the Wang family physicians on Lake Shang, a ritual for the distribution of food was held. When the invocation was being performed, a dark wind suddenly arose and all the lamps and candles were extinguished.

The attendants retreated to a distance, but [the master] remained single-mindedly focused on his visualization and recitation. In a mere instant, the lamps and candles were lit once more. After that, there was no longer any sound of wailing and weeping.
On the twenty-first, twenty-second, and twenty-third days, he gathered his disciples and lectured on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* three times. At that time, Jingchun...
When the Abbot came to the temple, he heard of this and saw both the ritual manual and the diagrams. Joining his palms, he exclaimed: "This is an envoy dispatched by Vairocana Buddha;
it is a meritorious achievement of the Patriarch Xianshou. Master Shenfu of Siming offered his congratulations, saying: "Your literary talent and conduct alone transcend the multitude;
your discourse is as vital as a whistling breeze, excelling in the ancient texts of India. You loftily continue the lotus lamp and share its wisdom-flame. Five clouds..."
Spreading colors to meet the clouds of compassion, a single drop from the spring of milk flows on without end. Branching out from the roots of the clouds, the stream becomes ever clearer;
may it well bestow the rain of Dharma upon the world, so that all three capacities, moistened by its grace, flourish in full splendor. (2) Zhaoqing Zhiqian sent this verse to Master Gong:
One cry recalls days of old; the "River Debate" already startled the multitude. Your karmic wisdom is loftier still, and your fragrant fame—

His fame spread even further, flowing through deep pools and transmitted to the Milk-Cave Grottoes; his teachings were as dense as rain and his compassion like gathering clouds. Traveling, he visited the places where the sutras were expounded, where heavenly flowers fell profusely upon his seat.

Furthermore, he composed thirty-eight fascicles of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra Commentary*, ten fascicles of the *Complete Exposition of the Laṅkāvatāra*, and lectured on the *Vajracchedikā* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Yu Wenxue Wei presented him with this verse: "The mind relies on the Buddha-fire; its nature is free from dust."
Alone I turned toward the Jeta Grove to cultivate the causes of stillness; fortunate was my attendance at the lecture hall, moistened by the nectar of the Dharma.

Deeply rejoicing that the fragrant altar was graced by the gentle breeze of wisdom, the Brahma-sounds descended from the nine heavens as the *buddha-pariṣad* flowers bloomed. In the second month, the spring harmony brought forth fresh willow colors. My failing strength laments that I heard the Way so late;
yet the Great Master, awakening the world, did not decline to teach repeatedly. Paṇ Wénxué’s carriage-bearer presented this gift, saying: "This humble chamber lies beside the clouds of compassion."

Morning and evening I am comforted by what I have heard; you rouse me and open the Deer Park for me. I have gained understanding and bid farewell to the flock of gulls, yet how can I bear that the assembly of enemies and kin makes it difficult to distinguish between gratitude and resentment?
I cherish your new writings, which must surely rescue us from the entanglements of the mundane world.

Sun Wenxue’s inscription of appreciation says: "I have heard the Unsurpassed Truth; its perfect realization is like the finest clarified butter (*sarpis*). The adept grasps its essence and, casting aside the trap, departs from the world."
Extraordinary! Recently I constructed the Blue Lotus Hall. I take up and play with the pearl within my breast; its radiance shines across the four fields.

How could it possibly be compared to *carma* or *jāmbūnada* gold? Beneath the eaves, benevolent birds sing; before the steps, red medicinal herbs bloom. White clouds rest upon the verdant trees; blue smoke rises from the purple *pǔ* grass.

It is as if I were meeting the cause of the Elephant King; it is like being amidst the initial falling of the flower-rain. My humble heart is filled with joy; I laugh at myself for being of this world.
The Confucian Zhao Xiaolian Liyuan presented this verse: "Within the Buddhist canon, thousands of volumes are arrayed; you dwell in quiet devotion within your small tower.

Seeing that you have no attachments, you wander freely among the white clouds. At the beginning of winter, a case of vomiting disease broke out, and he again dreamed of a deity clad in golden armor who said: [...the remainder of the text...]
If you wish to prolong your life and cure your illness, you may drink this elixir. Swallow it like lotus-root juice; a fragrance will emanate from within your mouth.

Upon waking, sores will appear all over your body, but within ten days, both ailments will be healed. (35) [This was written] while lecturing on the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* and the *Fivefold Teaching Ritual*. Mr.
Chu Tangzhou, a scholar of literature, invited me to perform the *xiànniàn* (commemorative recitation) rite. In a dream, his mother thanked him joyfully. — Recorded by Sun of Dongqingli.
When Wenxue Xiaozhen was performing the *Foyan* (Release of Flames) ritual, his young grandchildren saw their ancestors and various relatives all arriving together for the assembly;

they were struck with wonder and amazement. When Wenxue Tang Junfa’s wife, Lady Zhou, suffered from epilepsy as if possessed by a malevolent spirit, her delirious ravings ceased immediately upon the performance of a single rite of deliverance. (36)
I produced the forty-eight fascicles of the *Wujiaoyi Kezhu* (Annotated Outline of the Rituals of the Five Teachings), as well as the two chapters on the *Lianhua Jingdeng* (Lotus Mirror Lamp).

I gave thirty-seven lectures on the *Huayan Xuantan* (Prolegomena to the Avatamsaka Sutra). In the spring of the Wuma year, at the age of thirty-eight, I attended the Lotus Sutra lecture period at Juguang Temple;
my mother and son requested that I grant them the tonsure and administer the Three Refuges precepts. In the winter, I visited Vice-Governor Dai, Master Fuzhai.
At the Huayan Sutra Assembly, he composed one fascicle of a commentary and sub-commentary on the Śrī-mañjuśrī-buddhakṣetra-kuṭhāra-gāthā (the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra).
In the year Jiwu (1659), at the age of thirty-nine, he established a monastic community at Ciyun within his own temple. He expanded and enlarged the kitchen, storehouse, bathhouse, and latrines;

he settled the assembly in the meditation hall, dredged a pond for the release of living beings, lectured on the Lotus Sūtra during the spring, discussed the Awakening of Faith during the summer, initiated the Lánpén period for the Middle Primordial Festival, and established an unrestricted offering ceremony.

In the autumn of that year, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* was being performed. Zhi was among the assembly, hearing it directly from the master’s lips and subsequently lecturing upon it himself; at that time, he was esteemed as the foremost among the multitude.
He then produced two scrolls of the *Essentials of the Awakening of Faith* and eight scrolls of the *Compendium on the Ullambana Assembly*.

In his fortieth year, the Year of Gengshen, Governor Dai, because of the commentaries and records on the *Awakening of Faith*, each of which circulated as separate volumes, commissioned him to compile them into a unified edition for ease of consultation. Thereupon—

The combined twenty-four fascicles were compiled into ten fascicles, including one fascicle of topical outlines (*ke-wen*), one fascicle of the *Brief Record of the Fifth Patriarch*, and one fascicle of the *Illustrated Catalogue of Dharma Characteristics*.
Furthermore, he produced five fascicles of sub-commentaries on the *Sutra in Forty-two Sections*. He also solicited donations to carve the woodblocks for the *Ritual of the Five Teachings*.
Vice Governor Dai praised him, saying: "For twenty autumns his body has resided in the cloud-hall; in quiet reliance upon Chan contemplation, he ferries across the multitudes."

Raising his eyebrows, he joined only for the sake of discussing the sutras; walking with his medicine, he was instead detained by inquiries into its meaning. The source of the plum grove is inherently pure and not turbid;
who could rival you in cultivating the cursive script of the Cloud of Compassion? It has long been said that your virtue is profound and your merit vast;

at forty, you ascended the high seat, being the most eminent among your peers. Dai Changgong and Ren Chang prayed for a swift recovery from illness; you have carved the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* commentary and further requested to reside at Zifu Temple.
Yun took his leave and did not depart; he resided at Wénxué Gǔzhān. Admiring the profundity of the Dharma-gate of *anusmṛti* (mindfulness), he carved [the text] for its practice.
Forty-one: Wénxué Tiáoyuán dreamed that his wife requested a memorial service; after twenty-one days of *yoga*, five thousand lamps were offered as a transformation.

For five weeks, he maintained constant mindfulness and further transformed five thousand beings. During the interval of his nightly sleep, he saw the inhabitants of his chamber being led away by banners and music.

He composed five fascicles of commentaries on the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*. Furthermore, for the layman Wang Xinxian, he compiled one fascicle of the *Xizi Guijie* (The Western Aid for Receiving the Precepts).

He also carved woodblocks for three works—*Lianhuazhang*, *Jingdengzhang*, and *Duanzhengtu*—which were bound together in a single volume. [He also produced] the forty-two sections of the *Leng...* (likely the *Lengyan jing*).
Yan, together with the first two volumes of the *Shu-chao*, carved the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections* with its *Shu-chao*, as well as the *Wu-jiao-i kai-meng*.

In the spring of the forty-third year, he lectured on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*; in the summer, he annotated the second volume of the *Amitābha Sūtra*; and in the winter, he expounded the four volumes of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
In the forty-fourth spring of the *jiǎzǐ* year, you resided at Chongshou Monastery and inaugurated a *Vajracchedikā* lecture period;

there, you composed the six-fascicle sub-commentary on the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-sūtra* and carved the woodblocks for the *Direct Explanation of the Vajracchedikā*. In the winter, you went to Chaoyin Monastery in Deqing for a *Prajñāpāramitā* lecture period.
On the day of concluding the retreat, lay devotees invited him to remain; he declined their request two or three times.

On the fourth day of the fifth month (the *yichou* day), at age forty-five, he was to attend the summer lecture period on the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* at Yangmeiwu. He composed one fascicle of the *Ruyi Zhou Jing* (Sūtra of the Wish-Fulfilling Mantra) and transmitted the dharma of the monastic robe to five bhikṣus:
Changming Yuebiao, Zhiyi, Yaoyuan Yuefeng, Xian, Baoguo Yu'an, Cizhao, and Xingfu Yushan Lang. [He also entrusted it to] Chong'en.
The frown on his brow cleared. When the period of retreat concluded, the senior monks of the assembly requested that he take charge of the monastery’s permanent affairs;

he declined three times and refused to accept. At the beginning of summer, the two scholars Mr. Shi Gong of the Zhou family and Mr. Qian Zhi of the Military Bureau requested him to reside at Upper Zhushan.

During the Middle Yuan festival, the publication of the collated edition of the *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* was moved from the Dai Vice-Governor’s residence to the Lecture Hall of Ciyun Monastery for proofreading and carving. On the eighth month, the printing commenced.
I had the ritual for offering food (*śatrapūjā-vidhi*), the Commentary on the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, and the Text for Taking Refuge and Precepts carved into woodblocks.

In my forty-sixth year, the Year of Bingyin, I lectured on the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra*, entrusting two successors: first, Inamun of this temple; second, Deullimban of Jinjik.
At the end of autumn, Mr. Heotting Sosa, the Master of Astronomy, invited me to the quarters at Upper Zhihuashan (*Wangzhu*), where I subsequently compiled [this work].
One fascicle of the *Huayan Guanzizai Zhishi Zhang Ji* (Notes on the Chapter on the Spiritual Friend Avalokiteśvara of the Avataṃsaka). He revealed this to the fourfold assembly. [Year] Forty-seven:
In the spring, he inaugurated a lecture on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Three individuals received its transmission: Chongqing Ximinang, Nianhua Dazhenyin, and Wansong Erchengji.

In the seventh month, the combined edition of the *Qixinlun Shuji* (Commentary and Notes on the Awakening of Faith) was completed. [Year] Forty-eight: In the spring, he presided over the ordination platform.

During the Lotus Sūtra lecture period at the monastery, he separately authored one fascicle of commentaries on the *Vipaśyanā-vibhāga* (Chapter on Contemplating the Image). He also compiled one fascicle each for the *Ritual for Releasing Living Beings*, the *Ritual for Tonsure*, and the *Ritual for Returning to the Precepts*.

He edited two fascicles of the *Complete Collection of Various Sūtras for Recitation*. Furthermore, he carved ten fascicles of the annotated sub-commentary (*kēzhù*) on the *Wǔjiàoyí* (The Ritual of the Five Teachings).

In the spring of the year Jisi (1769), at the age of forty-nine, when Imperial Censor Shao Jie was serving as one of the Three Dukes, he followed the Emperor’s southern tour to the mountain and commanded the assembly to invite [the Master] to serve as abbot.
Thereupon, he lectured on the Diamond Sūtra, the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra, the Amitābha Sūtra, and the Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda Sūtra.

In the spring of the third month of the Gengwu year, at the age of fifty, [the Master] erected four stone pillars for the eaves in the front and rear halls of the Vairocana Rear Hall. He also constructed eight separate side rooms and enshrined statues of his teachers in the *zhangsì* (abbot’s quarters). Furthermore, he carved an inscription for the "Monument to the Restoration" and erected it at the Great [Hall]. *Gāngmíngkōngpǐn* (The Chapter on the Radiance of Emptiness), a commentary on the *Xīnjīngshū* (Commentary on the Heart Sutra) in three fascicles; and *Fǎjièguānjìngzhùzuàn* (Annotated Compilation of the Mirror of the Contemplation of the Dharma Realm) in two fascicles. He manifested a transformation and spoke these verses: "Upon the path of birth and death, I roam with ease and sovereignty; I am named Avalokiteśvara Buddha, reborn in the Lotus Realm.
Having received the Buddha’s prediction of enlightenment, I am perfectly enlightened and unimpeded; by the power of the Buddha’s vows, I shall deliver sentient beings for billions of years.

On the following day at noon, he bathed and took leave of the assembly. Sitting cross-legged with his hands joined at his chest, he passed away facing west. Six days later, when he was placed in the coffin, his complexion remained [radiant].
Upon his birth, a rare fragrance filled the chamber; ten thousand spectators beheld him, all prostrating themselves with tears falling as they hailed him as a Living Buddha.
Alas! Had it not been for his transcendent merit and practice, which moved those both near and far, why would there have been such longing during his life and such grief at his death?

At the age of forty, he opened the Dharma Hall and twice renovated the Great Amitābha Hall at Ciyun Temple, where he oversaw its consecration.
The images of the Four Heavenly Kings and the Three Sages; furthermore, in the year Dingyou, the rear hall was renovated and the Great Buddha of the "Welcoming Descent" (Jieyin) was newly enshrined.
I have heard that Ciyun founded this temple during the Tang dynasty, and since the Southern Song, over nine hundred years have passed.

It may be said that it has endured many years and for a long time; yet the Master, with his singular effort, restored it so that it would not fall into ruin. How magnificent is his achievement! Other...
For instance, he rebuilt the Shengguo Renshou Monastery and repaired numerous other Buddhist temples, so many that one’s fingers could not count them all.
Previously, in the spring of the *Kangxi* year *Yichou*, Zhou Gong, Palace Librarian, and Ren Gong, Minister of War, invited the Master to Yangmei Wu to lecture on the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
Not long thereafter,

when the Sacred Ancestor, Emperor Renhuang, was on his southern tour, the Grand Secretary, Duke Shao, led the assembly with due ceremony to invite him into the abbot’s quarters, where they respectfully welcomed him.

Regarding the Imperial Visits: Entrusting the completion of the Vairocana Hall construction, His Majesty visited the site five times, from the thirty-eighth year to the forty-sixth year of the Kangxi era.
He was bestowed with abundant gifts and honors.
An imperial inscription was composed for him to eternally enshrine the sacred mountain.
Successively, he was granted plaques, the Heart Sūtra, the *Bao ta yaoshi jing* (Precious Pagoda Bhaisajyaguru Sūtra), and praises for the Diamond Sūtra.

His gracious rewards were ever-increasing and never-ending. Furthermore, coinciding with this, Lord Wang, the Commander of the River, donated fifteen hundred taels of his own salary. Within less than two years, the Vairocana Hall was completed.

The Master ascended the seat and lectured on the *Amitābha Sūtra*, the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the *Śāriputra-requital-of-Gratitude Sūtra*, the "Universal Gate" chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra*, the "Avalokiteśvara" chapter of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, the "Emptiness" chapter of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*, and others.
The people of good character were moved by faith and admiration, joyfully providing much assistance in gold. The Master further fashioned ten [statues].

Regarding the images of the Six Princes and the reconstruction of the Brahma-temple (Buddhist monastery), the Master’s restoration of Upper Zhushan is such that it is difficult to describe its excellence in full.

After six years had passed, the Master wished to retire from the monastery. The local gentry, officials, and elders submitted a formal petition earnestly requesting him to remain. The Master said, "To unworthily occupy the abbot's quarters is not what is fitting for a son of the Buddha.
He then took his leave and returned to Renshou, where he continued to dwell in a secluded small room, subsisting on wood-fiber food and grass.

As for his robes: he wore a single patched garment for ten years and a single pair of sandals for three years. For fifty springs and autumns, his hands never ceased turning over the pages of scripture.
He produced more than six hundred fascicles of commentary and annotation. When people saw him suddenly, they did not realize he was one who sat upon a dharma-seat to preach the Dharma.

I recall that in the past, there was a hermitage called Desheng on the Broken Bridge of West Lake, which served as the master’s place for quiet retreat; it was originally established by the elder Qian Ruoyan.
Master Fuzi, Grand Historian Mao, the Reverend Mr. Xiao, Master Zhou Yun, his father’s mentor, as well as my elder brother Dongbiao, Mengshi, and others presided over these affairs.

All matters—such as the offering of sacrifices to the sages, the burial of exposed bones, the release of living creatures, the ancestral offerings, and the salvation of orphaned spirits—were carried out according to these principles.

Master Shi composed the *Eryi Pian* (Treatise on the Two Principles) to record these events. Now that the Master’s years have grown advanced, we look forward to the continued practice [of these rites].
Carrying a gourd and wearing a bamboo hat, he faced the wall at the edge of the world for the rest of his life, doing nothing more than being a man of no affairs.

Who would have thought that in the spring of the *Xin-chou* year of the Kangxi era, Upper Zhi Temple would suffer from the calamity of fire? Consequently, the bells and drums of the Holy Mountain fell silent, and the towers and terraces of the Precious Site were entirely reduced to ashes.
Alas! The master’s心血 (*xīnxiě*, blood and heart/mind) accumulated over several years was, in a single instant, utterly consumed by the flames.

Ding. With tears falling and hearts grieved, how can this be adequately described? We cannot help but once again invite the Dharma-rain from the Compassionate Clouds, looking up with longing toward Master Yuanyong.
For this reason, twenty-eight people, including Wuci and others, have first submitted this petition to the local authorities and the various gentry and scholars.
At that time, there were also the Vice Minister Tang and the Academician Chen of the Hanlin Academy.

Xu, the Provincial Education Commissioner; Wang, the Censor-in-Chief; and over thirty other officials, along with more than sixty fellow scholars from the three academies, petitioned the Great Master to enter the mountain to preside over its reconstruction.
The Master then established regulations and strategies, and the assembly became clear in their understanding of the Buddha-dharma.
Regarding the extensive cultivation of fields of merit through giving: those who planted the Jetavana Grove by spreading gold over its grounds have followed one after another in this tradition.

From the summer solstice of the *xinchou* year to the spring of the *wushen* year, [the site contained] the pavilions and terraces of the Great Being’s imperial palace, the incense altar of the traveling residence, the West Meditation Hall, the North Guest Quarters, the East Temple of the *Gārala*, and the Patriarchal [Hall].
Master, the halls of Kṣitigarbha and the Heavenly Kings each had their doors and windows laid out; the planning and arrangement were largely completed.
Your contribution was indeed great, and your dedication was truly arduous.
In the year of Renyin, the Emperor bestowed four dragon-eye bodhi seeds, which were planted therein.
To the left and right of the Hall of the Great Being (Mahāsattva), the Master respectfully composed one chapter of verse to extol this boundless grand ceremony.
Now that our Emperor has ascended the throne...

The Great Being was a compassionate father to the people. During droughts and floods, his prayers were invariably answered. In the first year of the Yongzheng era, he was specially commissioned by the Emperor to offer incense;
in the second year, he was ordered to repair the ancestral pagoda at Mount Qing.
Both of these matters were brought about through the Master’s silent, profound sincerity. It is a pity that when the work was nearing completion, [the Master passed away].
The Master has already returned to the West; this is truly lamentable. The Master was born on the eleventh day of the tenth month in the fourteenth year of the Chongzheng era at the hour of Xu.
His worldly lifespan was eighty-eight years, and his monastic seniority was seventy-nine years. The general outline of his life was such that his mind never deviated from [the Dharma].

The nature of the Tathāgata’s instruction is unstained by the burdens of worldly dust; his physical being is undiminished. As for the outward conduct of a śramaṇa, he does not contravene the scriptures of the Vinaya:
his eyes do not gaze upon what is improper, his mouth does not consume rich delicacies, and his hands do not let go of his prayer beads.
His sides did not brush against the dust; his feet did not tread upon deviant paths. When lodging, he was never apart from his robes and bowl.
He entered the mire without being defiled; he dwelt in turbidity without being muddied. He propagated the Dharma-gate through purity and took wisdom as the fruit of merit.

He was earnest in saving those beyond [the world] and diligent in universally ferrying others across. He did not exalt himself for a single practice, nor did he claim credit for a single achievement for others.
To those who sought refuge, he went to them unbidden; to those who sought spiritual benefit, he would instruct them before they had even reached a state of frustration.
Though they were young and immature, he never discriminated against them in his reception; though they were arrogant and headstrong, he never hesitated to guide and transform them.
Truly, he was an emanation of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, a model for all sentient beings. The Master served as the successor to Deshui for sixty years. All...
Upon the passing of the anniversary of his death, he would invariably attend in person to sweep the stupa and make offerings with due ritual propriety. He did not merely avoid negligence;
rather, he treated him as if he were still alive, never forgetting his teacher’s instructions. Furthermore, those to whom he transmitted the robe and the Dharma were Changming, Yuebiao, and Yaoyuan.
Yuefeng, Renshou, Xuru, Caoyuan, Kejiu, Bayu, Jianmei, Donglai, Hongyuan, and Baoguo.
Yuan'an, Xingfu, Yushan, Masan, Mo'wen, Fengshan, Mingzang, Nianhua, Dazhen, and Beijing.
Tixian, Ciyun, Qinan, Shangzhu, Peifeng, Ciyi, Zhengzhong, Tianhuai, and others—counting more than twenty people in total.
As for their years of monastic seniority (*śrāmaṇera*), they cannot all be recorded. Among the scriptures they authored are twelve works, including the *Huayan biexing jing yuantan shu caoji*;
twenty-five works, including the *Lengyan jing xu shi yuantan shu*; and [works by] Xian...

*Shou wu jiao yi* (The Ritual for the Five Teachings), six fascicles; *Ke zhu* (Annotated Commentary), forty-eight fascicles; *Qixin lun shu ji hui yue* (A Comparative Review of Commentaries and Records on the Awakening of Faith), ten fascicles;

*Yaoshi shu chao* (Commentary and Sub-commentary on the Medicine Master Sūtra), six fascicles; *Guanyin shu chao* (Commentary and Sub-commentary on the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra), eight fascicles; *Jingang zhi jie* (Direct Explanation of the Diamond Sūtra), five fascicles;

*Sishier zhang jing shu chao* (Commentary and Sub-commentary on the Sūtra in Forty-two Sections), five fascicles; *Guanjing zhizhi shu* (Direct Pointing Commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra), ten fascicles; and the *Yujia shishi jing* (Yogācāra Sūtra on the Bestowal of Food).

Ten commentaries: the Commentary on the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra; the Brief Notes on the Amitābha Sūtra; the Commentary on the *Cintāmaṇicakra-dhāraṇī*; the Two Explanations of the Heart Sūtra; the Commentary on the Uṣṇīṣavijayā Dhāraṇī Sūtra;

the Sub-commentary on the Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra; the Commentary on the Chapter on Contemplating the Image; the Explanation of the Sūtra on the Eightfold Mindfulness of the Mahāsattvas; and the Explanation of the Great Compassion Dhāraṇī.
*Commentary on the Cundī Dhāraṇī*, one fascicle each; *The Fundamental Principles of the Buddhas and Patriarchs*, four fascicles; *The Ten Essentials of the Virtuous School*, two fascicles;

*Record of the Causes and Effects of Recitation*; *Record of Various Signs of Mindfulness of the Buddha*; *Verses on the Pure Land of Sukhāvatī*; *Wholesome Words for Awakening the World*; *Rite for Taking Refuge and Receiving Precepts for the Western Assistance*;
*Yogic Rite for Taking Refuge and Receiving Precepts*; *Rite for Chanting for the Deceased*; *Rite for Releasing Living Beings*, one fascicle each; and *Rite for the Feeding of Hungry Ghosts*.
There are ten volumes of commentaries (*shū*) and one volume of annotated excerpts on the *Yankou* (Feeding the Hungry Ghosts), totaling one hundred and sixty-eight volumes.
In the autumn of the Jihai year, my elder brother Dongbiao provided the funds and dispatched me to deposit these into the collection at Lengyan Temple.
Lord Wu, the Prefect of Jiahe County, composed a preface for them so that future seekers might find them. Those not yet committed to woodblocks total one hundred and twenty-six volumes.
All of these were compiled by Master Li over many years; I witnessed this with my own eyes. Alas, in the year of Xinchou (1821), Yunfang was consumed by fire and reduced to ashes.
Since the disaster caused by the god of fire, there have been several works he annotated and had carved for printing that had not yet been included in the Tripitaka.

For instance, the *Fahua Yuantan Kezhu* (Commentary on the Essential Discourse of the Lotus Sutra) in seventeen fascicles, which he commissioned me to transcribe by hand and requested an explanation for, led to Dharma Master Wen’i composing a preface. Thus...
In the sixtieth year of the Kangxi era, Li Rian Kalin sent [the texts] to the capital for deposit at Nan Guanyin Temple.
He further exhorted the Dharma Master Paitian to solicit donations for carving woodblocks so that they might circulate.

Furthermore, there are three volumes each of the *Myriad Buddhas Repentance*, the *Requital of Kindness Repentance*, the *Amitābha Repentance*, the *Seven Buddhas Bhaisajyaguru Repentance*, and the revised *Guanyin Repentance*, along with the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra: Separately Circulating Chapters*. Conveniently...
For the four assemblies, there is a daily liturgy and recitation manual preserved at Zhaokong Temple.

Furthermore, there are four collections consisting of the *Vajracchedikā-sūtra* with the *Kaīmēng* commentary, the *Ārya-śraddhā-prakaraṇa* with the *Kāidào* commentary, the *Bodhicittotpāda-śāstra* with the *Kāiwù* commentary, and the *Heart Sūtra* with the *Kaīmēng* commentary; these allow those of the Three Vehicles to understand them at a glance.

Additionally, there are the *Records of Upper Zhushan*, the *Records of Ciyun*, the *Records of Renshou*, and the *Records of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, all of which are preserved in their respective temples. Moreover, [this work] was composed last winter.

The *Renhuang Chan* (Repentance for the Benevolent Sovereign) in three fascicles was composed to commemorate the inconceivable and vast grace of the imperial ancestors; the *Baocan Chan* (Repentance for Protecting Silkworms) in three fascicles was composed to ensure the welfare of the myriad people through seasonal harmony and bountiful harvests.
The drafts of these remain in my study. However, it is only the commentary on the Huayan school of Buddhism from the fourth year of the Yongzheng era that remains.
This work, in fourteen fascicles, has not yet been carved for printing.
It traces the origins and development from the Buddha and the patriarchs down to the present day, examining and extracting from the *Tripiṭaka* all points of debate, disagreement, and consensus.
It is not intended merely to advocate for the Xianshou school; rather, no other school fails to benefit from it. Thus, it serves as a ford for later students to enter the Way of virtue.
It was indeed a matter of great regret that while the transcription, collation, and editing were just being finalized, the Master suddenly passed away at Upper Zhushan.

It must now be committed to woodblocks, awaiting future inclusion in the canon so that it may endure imperishably. Furthermore, he once composed a preface for the Four Books and a preface for the *Explanation of Seal Characters*.
His *Gangjian*, *Suibiji*, *Wendao shuo*, and *Juemilu* all delve deeply into the principles of human nature (*xingli*), sufficient to demonstrate that he was a versatile Confucian scholar.
It is a pity, however, that he ended his life as a Buddhist monk. Alas! The Master had already reached the age of eighty or ninety;

yet, when he sat by a lamp to compile his commentaries, though the characters were as small as fly’s feet, there were rarely any deletions or corrections. He once said to me: "Whenever I am engaged in the vast task of annotation..."
[The text was] extensive; [I have here] abridged it. For a brief moment with eyes closed, the nectar of consecration descended, and my divine thoughts surged forth like a gale.

With rapid brushstrokes, the composition was completed without the need for deliberation. Alas! All of this is due to the Master’s long-cultivated, perfectly luminous wisdom. My mind and the Master’s have been in perfect accord.

Over several decades, we have shared the longest friendship and the deepest mutual understanding. Were it not for the Master, who else could have discerned me? Were it not for me, there would be no means to record the Master’s life.
Therefore, unaware that my words were flowing so profusely, I have recorded them in great detail.

Even a single annotated fact is sufficient to continue the past and open the way for the future, establishing a comprehensive canon unprecedented throughout the ages. It may be called the founding patriarch of an era;
it would not be improper to call him the founding patriarch of a thousand or ten thousand generations. This is the Master’s [teaching].
The manifestations of his spiritual power and extraordinary wonders are truly too numerous to enumerate. Herein, I have selected the principal points and composed this inscription, saying:

"I have heard that among the myriad forms of life, each possesses its own inherent nature. Humans suffer because they have not yet perceived it; even when they perceive it, they do not exhaustively realize it.

How magnificent is the Great Master! His merit and wisdom were predestined from of old. Having received the entrustment at Milk Peak (Nanyue), he subsequently transmitted the Mind-Seal. He is the direct successor of the Lotus Pond (Zhuhong)."

The vehicle of the Holy Head (Bhadramukha) school shines its divine light upward; thus it is called "Consecration" (Abhiṣeka). The Tripiṭaka masters awaken the deluded, while the five families offer profound reflection.
The flying staff of the Cloud of Compassion brings prosperity to the Brahma temples; the banner is raised at Upper Zhuchi, and the jade palaces are restored to order.
When food was offered, ghosts and spirits withdrew; when the Dharma was preached, fish and dragons emerged to listen.

Having received the profound favor of the Sacred Court, you became an object of faith and reverence for both officials and commoners. For eighty-eight years, your merit was perfected and the fruit of realization attained.
Do not say that you are like a bright mirror; why have you suddenly vanished? If a single thing is fundamentally non-existent, what use is there for reflection? Do not say it is empty.
The valley is silent; though one knocks, there is no response. All phenomena are empty. Only after awakening does one become enlightened.
Plucking leaves and grasping flowers, striking the wind and chasing shadows—these vanish like clouds dispersing and waters flowing away, leaving the sky vast and the moon serene.
The Great Master Guanding of Upper Tianzhu entrusted these words of dharma:
"In the Confucian school, there are the Four Companions; in the Buddha-dharma, there are the Four Disciples. There are the Four Worthies of Kumārajīva and the Four Attainers of Bodhidharma.
The Lamp of Wisdom had eight princes, and Zhisheng had sixteen grandsons; all of them left home as *kumārabhūta* and attained the Way as *śrāmaṇeras*. This continues down to..."
At the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings all engaged in calculation and deliberation.

My ancestor, the Great Master Yunqi, traveled north to visit the Lord Teacher Bianrong, who bestowed upon him the practice of sincere *nianfo* (mindfulness of the Buddha). He was instructed to follow the Way according to the Buddha’s teachings, not to covet fame or profit, and never to pursue worldly conditions.

As the successor to the patriarchal robe and the seal of the Dharma, he opened the gate of the Pure Land school; his commentaries and sub-commentaries on the *Amitābha Sūtra* caused the Lotus sect to spread far and wide.

Zhen. My late master Dezu inherited the Dharma-seal of our Buddha. He received the lineage from afar through five generations and subsequently resided at Upper Zhuchi. The hall of the abbot’s quarters had fallen into ruin;

he initiated its restoration with two distinct approaches. His lectures and commentaries on the scriptures were numerous beyond measure. Indeed, Mount Lingjiu in India was always abundant with men of outstanding talent.
Before the altar of the Great Being, these four eminent masters stand at the forefront. Some serve as teachers of men; others provide models through the Vinaya.

Their reputations are renowned afar as they sustain and flourish the sacred incense and lamps. Following me in this turning of the wheel, they are truly worthy of my final entrustment: the Buddha is the mind, and this mind is the Buddha.
At Yunqi, the seeds of the Buddha were never severed; at Wufeng and Changshui, the torch of the Dharma blazed brightly.
Ascending the precious throne and the dragon bed of the Holy Patriarchs, the ancestral seal for delivering sentient beings has been transmitted and entrusted down through the ages.

The lamp-pyramid of the Benevolent Sovereign has been brought forth upon the incense table; it illuminates the imperial destiny of the world, ensuring its stability and far-reaching prosperity. Now, through this Dharma-garment, I entrust it to you, Tenpō.
You four shall be fixed as the successors, receiving and transmitting it in turn just as the five hundred arhats did in the past, without any difference.
Others are many and talented; let us wait for future conditions. Thus it was said.
Entrusted to the foremost Dharma-son, Peifeng (one statue of the Buddha and one red robe). (Seal) [Hidden Buddha].
The treasury of knowledge and vision does not come from without; the crest-jewel atop the Buddha’s head is entirely attained through one's own merit-base and life of wisdom.
Nurtured by the warmth of spring, the spiritual sprouts of the seeds of intelligence flourish and bear fruit.
Among the great principles of the Five Elements, there is none that does not blaze with brilliance.
The Second Son, Jieyi, Entrusted with the Dharma (one statue of the Buddha and one purple robe).
Born from the Buddha’s own mouth, Following the Buddha in conduct, Having attained the Buddha-Dharma, Truly a son of the Great Being;
Strictly purifying the Vinaya, Realizing Perfect Enlightenment, Transmitting the Holy Contemplation of Mind, He upholds the Buddha-Dharma.
His ritual conduct models the Three Realms; his compassion flourishes for a hundred generations.
Entrustment to the Third Son, Zhengzhong (one censer, one incense burner).
His literary talent rivals You and Xia; his eloquence surpasses Cai and Gong; his administrative affairs match Ji and Ran; his virtuous conduct equals Bo and Zhong.

Possessing the single body of the Sage, there is the vast and sudden Great Function. Just as Yi taught people archery by having them practice within the bowstring, so too does the Great Being’s Way encompass every matter with perfect penetration.
This is the Fourth Entrustment to Tianhuai: (one staff, one shoe).

Heaven was born in me, enabling me to cherish brilliant virtue; I shall succeed the Buddha to propagate the Way. With profound wisdom and skillful eloquence regarding the Yin-Yang and the Lü-lü, I adapt and harmonize according to the capacities of beings.
Above and below are reconciled in harmony; The Ruler rejoices and the people bask in his grace as I transform the realm within.
Thus I accord with the heart and mind of the Emperor.

In obedience to the Master’s command, I washed my hands and wrote this notification for the entire mountain community. It was the twenty-ninth day of the third month in the sixth year of the Yongzheng era, a Jimao day.
